title: Compliance, Data Protection, and Securing AI Workloads
bodyMarkdown:
## Shared responsibility, and why a provider certificate is not yours

Compliance on Google Cloud is shared. The [shared responsibility and shared fate documentation](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate) splits duties by service model:

- **IaaS** (Compute Engine, Cloud Storage): Google secures the infrastructure; you carry most application, configuration, and data-protection duties.
- **PaaS** (App Engine, GKE): Google takes on more, but you still own application-level controls, IAM, and your data.
- **SaaS** (Google Workspace) and **FaaS:** Google owns most controls; you remain responsible for access and the data you put in.

The practical consequence: Google's audit reports and certifications attest to Google's controls over its infrastructure and services. They do **not** make your application compliant, so a SaaS startup asked for a SOC 2 report still needs its **own** audit covering its application, access management, change management, and operations. Google's report is evidence you can inherit controls from, not a substitute.

"Shared fate" is Google's extension: secure blueprints, Security Command Center Premium, Organization Policies, and Confidential Computing, plus a cyber-insurance program.

## Regimes mapped to controls

| Regime / data type | What drives the design | Typical controls |
|---|---|---|
| **HIPAA** (PHI) | Execute a BAA, use only covered services, no PHI in unsupported places | CMEK, Data Access audit logs, least-privilege IAM, VPC-SC, restricted log sinks |
| **PCI DSS** (card data) | Minimize where raw PANs exist to shrink scope | Sensitive Data Protection tokenization, network segmentation, logging, key management |
| **GDPR** (EU personal data) | Lawful processing, data-subject access and erasure, residency choices | Data processing terms (DPA), location constraints, Sensitive Data Protection discovery and classification |
| **Data sovereignty** | Data location **and** who can access it | Assured Workloads control package plus location org policy, key control (CMEK/EKM) |
| **SOC 2 / audits** | Evidence of controls over time | Audit logs to an immutable restricted (locked) sink, SCC posture reports and history, change records |

### HIPAA specifics

The [HIPAA documentation](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa) states the rules that questions probe. You must determine whether you are a Covered Entity or Business Associate and, if so, accept the **BAA** through the "Privacy compliance and records for Google Cloud" support page. The BAA covers Google's infrastructure and 200+ services, including BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, Logging and Monitoring. You may **not** use unsupported services or pre-GA offerings with PHI, and the customer must configure everything else. Documented restrictions include: no PHI in resource metadata or monitoring labels, Identity Platform custom attributes or Cloud Build configuration, and keep Speech-to-Text data logging disabled. Signing the BAA is necessary, not sufficient.

## Data ownership, GDPR and children's data

**Ownership.** Google's [Enterprise Privacy Commitments](https://cloud.google.com/privacy) state that customer data is yours: processed only according to your agreements, never sold or used for ad profiles, and backed by the Cloud Data Processing Addendum. Per the [GDPR page](https://cloud.google.com/privacy/gdpr) Google deletes it within a maximum of **180 days** of a complete deletion instruction unless retention obligations apply. You decide why data is processed, so you remain the controller.

**GDPR.** Google commits contractually to GDPR for its processing, handles data only on your instructions, publishes subprocessors, and offers EU standard contractual clauses for transfers outside the EU. **You** answer data-subject requests to access, rectify, restrict or delete data. That is why discovery matters: erasure fails for data you cannot locate, including copies in backups, logs and exports. Region choice is not a lawful basis on its own.

**COPPA** (US, children under 13) applies to operators of services directed at children, or with actual knowledge they collect a child's personal information. For your own app on Google Cloud you are the operator ([COPPA page](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/coppa)), and the provider cannot certify compliance for you. Design for minimization: collect less, de-identify with Sensitive Data Protection, set retention and deletion, and keep children's data out of analytics and ad pipelines.

## Privacy operations: erasure and storage limitation

Two duties that security controls do not satisfy (design guidance, not legal advice).

- **Erasure** (GDPR [Article 17](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) and similar US state deletion rights): a **verified** request obliges the controller to delete or irreversibly anonymize that person's data **without undue delay** in **every** store: databases, analytics copies, exports, caches and backups.
- **Storage limitation:** each data category gets a retention period tied to its purpose, and **automated deletion** runs when it ends. Parking everything in a Coldline archive "just in case" lowers cost but is still indefinite retention.

| Store | Automated deletion | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Storage | [Lifecycle](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) `Delete` rules (age, noncurrent versions) | Asynchronous; blocked by unexpired retention policies and holds |
| BigQuery | Table or partition expiration, DML `DELETE` | [Time travel](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/time-travel) keeps changed or deleted data 7 days by default (2 to 7), then a fixed 7-day fail-safe that only Cloud Customer Care can open |
| Spanner | [Row deletion policy (TTL)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/ttl) | Typically within 72 hours; earlier backups still hold the rows |
| Firestore | [TTL policy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/docs/ttl) | Typically within 24 hours; expired documents stay queryable until deleted |
| Bigtable | [Garbage collection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/garbage-collection) by age | Up to a week |
| Cloud SQL | No native row TTL in the docs reviewed: scheduled `DELETE` jobs or partition drops | [Automated backups](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups) keep 1 to 365 days; on-demand backups persist until deleted |

Cloud Storage [soft delete](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/soft-delete) is on by default: deleted objects stay recoverable for 7 days (configurable 7 to 90; 0 disables) and lifecycle rules cannot purge them early. Count that window in your erasure commitment, or disable it on personal-data buckets. (BigQuery expiration versus retention: see mod-provision-03.)

**Backups** need a bounded retention window so erased subjects age out; re-apply a deletion ledger after any restore, or it resurrects them. Google's own [deletion process](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/deletion) takes about two months for active systems and up to about 180 days overall, backups included.

**What does not satisfy erasure:**

- **Audit logs** record who touched data; they delete nothing and can hold personal data themselves.
- **VPC Service Controls** limit exfiltration paths, not how long data lives.
- **CMEK alone** encrypts at rest; the data stays readable to anyone the key serves. Destroying a key makes everything under it unrecoverable (default [scheduled destruction](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kms/docs/destroy-restore) is 30 days, cancelable until then). That is **crypto-shredding**, and it fits only when the erasure unit equals the key unit, such as one key **per tenant** when offboarding a tenant. A key per end user across millions of rows is heavy to operate, and plaintext copies (exports, caches, derived tables) survive.

**Erasure versus legal retention.** Erasure is not absolute: [Article 17(3)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) allows processing to continue where needed for a legal obligation or for establishing or defending legal claims. Classify records by retention class: erasable data is deleted on request; records under a statutory duty or legal hold are kept, restricted to that purpose, and deleted automatically when the duty ends. A locked retention policy enforces such a duty irreversibly (the bucket cannot be deleted until every object fulfils its retention), so keep erasable personal data **out** of locked buckets. Counsel decides the classes.

## Sensitive Data Protection

Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP; the API is still the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API) has four capabilities, per the [overview](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitive-data-protection-overview):

- **Discovery:** data profiles across an organization to find where sensitive data lives.
- **Inspection:** deep scans of specific resources for sensitive instances (infoTypes).
- **De-identification:** masking, redaction, bucketing, date shifting, and tokenization.
- **Risk analysis:** re-identification risk in structured data.

**Inspect versus de-identify.** Inspection only finds and reports; de-identification transforms the data. Locating card numbers calls for inspection or discovery; an analytics-safe copy calls for de-identification. [Image redaction](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/redacting-sensitive-data-images) uses OCR to cover text in JPEG, BMP and PNG images but does not support PDF files.

The [pseudonymization documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization) is the key to the PCI question. Three methods are available: **deterministic encryption (AES-SIV)**, reversible but not preserving length or character set; **format-preserving encryption (FPE-FFX)**, reversible and preserving both; and **cryptographic hashing (HMAC-SHA-256)**, one-way. All three give **referential integrity**: the same key and context tweak always produce the same token, so analytics joins still work. Use **Cloud KMS wrapped keys** (recommended), not raw unwrapped keys in production. So for "replace PANs with surrogate values that still join," the answer is format-preserving tokenization, not encrypting the whole table or relying on firewall rules.

| Need | Technique |
|---|---|
| Hide value permanently, no joins | Redaction or masking |
| Joins and analytics on tokens, one-way | HMAC-SHA-256 hashing |
| Joins plus ability to reverse for authorized workflows | AES-SIV or FPE-FFX with a KMS-wrapped key |
| Token must look like the original (length, digits) | FPE-FFX |
| Coarsen numeric or date detail | Bucketing, date shifting |
| Know where sensitive data is | Discovery profiles |

## Residency and sovereignty

Two controls, with different jobs. The [Assured Workloads overview](https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/overview) describes a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls. Packages fall into **regional data boundaries** (EU, US, UK and others), **regulatory data boundaries** (FedRAMP, CJIS, IL2/IL4/IL5, ITAR, healthcare), and **Sovereign Controls by Partners**. It enforces them with Organization Policy constraints at the **folder** level, restricts storage location, controls which Google personnel handle support (Assured Support), supports CMEK or Cloud EKM depending on package, and monitors for violations.

`constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` is narrower. The [defining locations page](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/defining-locations) says it limits where **new** resources are created for supported services, and is **not** a data residency commitment. Therefore: a requirement that data **and the personnel who can access it** stay in the EU maps to **Assured Workloads (EU Regions and Support) plus** the location constraint, not to a single EU multi-region bucket and not to the constraint alone.

## Securing AI workloads

Generative AI adds attack surfaces: prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful content, malicious URLs in prompts or responses, and sensitive-data leakage. [Model Armor](https://cloud.google.com/model-armor/docs/overview) screens both **prompts and responses**:

- **Prompt injection and jailbreak** detection, with blocking when detected.
- **Malicious URL** detection (up to 256 URLs per request).
- **Responsible AI filters** for hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit and dangerous content.
- **Sensitive Data Protection integration** to flag PII, financial data, and credentials.
- **Document screening** (PDF, Office files, CSV, TXT, up to 4 MB).

Behavior is controlled by **templates** with confidence thresholds: **High**, **Medium and above**, or **Low and above** (more false positives). Use separate templates for input and output. **Inspect only** logs detections without blocking, which is the safe way to tune; **Inspect and block** enforces. **Floor settings** set organization-wide minimum protections across all templates. Model Armor is stateless and integrates with Vertex AI, Gemini Enterprise, Apigee, GKE via Service Extensions, and MCP servers.

**Deploying the model securely.** Reuse earlier controls (least-privilege IAM per agent, Secret Manager, audit logs, Binary Authorization for custom serving containers), then add the AI-specific ones. The product is Vertex AI, branded in current docs as Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

- **Network isolation.** The [VPC-SC guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/vpc-service-controls) says these APIs are reachable from the internet by default (IAM still applies), and Private Service Connect for Google APIs or Private Google Access does not remove that public path. A VPC-SC perimeter blocks public access to training data, models, inference requests and batch results; reach it privately via the restricted VIP.
- **Private serving.** The [Private Service Connect endpoint guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/private-service-connect) recommends dedicated private endpoints for custom and AutoML models needing private, low-latency access: no public IP, no peered range, default request timeout 10 minutes.
- **CMEK.** Per the [CMEK guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/cmek), the key covers training VM disks, dataset items, stored models and endpoint model files, but not metadata such as names or in-memory data, and it does **not** configure Cloud Storage, Artifact Registry or Logging for you.
- **Model vetting.** By default anyone with access can deploy any Model Garden model. The [`vertexai.allowedModels` constraint](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/control-model-access) restricts `publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL:ACTION` for `predict`, `deploy` and `tune`; an allow list implicitly denies the rest, explicit deny beats allow, models are listed one by one (max 500 values), and models in Model Registry are out of scope. Treat open models as third-party code.

Model Armor is the only control here that understands **prompt and response content**; an edge WAF or DDoS control does not.

### Secure AI Framework (SAIF)

**What it is.** SAIF is Google's conceptual framework for securing AI systems through their lifecycle. It is guidance, not a service you enable. The [SAIF overview](https://safety.google/intl/en/safety/saif/) names **six core elements**, which are not a sequence: expand strong security foundations to the AI ecosystem; extend detection and response to bring AI into your threat universe; automate defenses; harmonize platform-level controls; adapt controls with faster feedback loops; contextualize AI risks in surrounding business processes.

| Core element | Google Cloud controls that implement it |
|---|---|
| Foundations | IAM, VPC Service Controls, Org Policy, CMEK |
| Detection and response | Cloud Audit Logs, Security Command Center with AI Protection |
| Automate defenses | Org-wide guardrails such as Model Armor floor settings and Org Policy |
| Harmonize platform controls | One policy baseline set at organization or folder level |
| Adapt controls | Model Armor inspect-only tuning, red-team results fed back into templates |
| Contextualize risk | Per-use-case risk assessment, such as SAIF's risk self-assessment |

The right-hand column is a study aid, not an official Google table.

**Risk map.** The [SAIF guidance](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/cloud-ciso-perspectives-practical-guidance-building-with-saif) describes four AI system components (**data, infrastructure, model, application**) and groups controls the same way. Data controls on Google Cloud include IAM, bucket and dataset access controls, and Dataplex; model controls include a dedicated AI firewall such as Model Armor, Gemini as a guard model, and Apigee as an API gateway; application controls secure the interface between user and model. Assurance and governance controls apply to all risks.

**Use it** as the checklist for an AI security design review, then pick products per gap. **Anti-pattern:** treating SAIF as a product, or buying one control (an AI firewall) and calling the framework done.

## Audits and continuous compliance evidence

Auditors want evidence over time. Enable [audit logs](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) (Data Access for PHI and PII, since it is off by default except BigQuery), route them through an org-level aggregated sink to a restricted destination, and use Security Command Center to monitor posture against frameworks such as NIST, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS.

A SOC 2 Type I report assesses control design at one date. **Type II** also tests that controls **operated** across a review period (typically months), sampling records from the whole period, so evidence must be generated and kept continuously. A report produced the week before the audit shows state then, not operation over time.

| Evidence | Google Cloud source | Over-time caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Who did what | [Audit logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit): Admin Activity always on; Data Access off by default except BigQuery | `_Default` keeps 30 days (`_Required` 400, fixed). Route through an org aggregated sink to a [log bucket with locked retention](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets) (1 to 3,650 days; locking is irreversible) |
| Misconfigurations and fixes | Security Command Center findings and framework posture | [BigQuery export](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-analyze-findings-in-big-query) adds each finding and update as rows: your history |
| Resource and IAM changes | [Cloud Asset Inventory](https://docs.cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/overview) history | Kept 35 days; export snapshots on a schedule |
| Access reviews | [IAM Recommender](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/recommender-overview) (up to 90 days of usage) | The recommendation is not evidence; the record that someone reviewed and acted is |
| Change management | Pipeline records: reviewed merges, approvals, deploy audit entries | Changes outside the pipeline are what auditors find |
| Control checks | [Audit Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/audit-manager/docs/overview) with its SOC 2 framework assesses resource configuration | Each run is a snapshot: repeat it (scheduled audits are Preview), keep every report; some controls need manual review |

These support an audit; the independent auditor certifies.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Treating the BAA as compliance.** It is the contractual start; covered services, CMEK, logging, and access control are still required.
- **Using non-covered or pre-GA services for PHI**, or putting PHI in labels.
- **Using `gcp.resourceLocations` alone for sovereignty**, or expecting it to relocate resources.
- **Encrypting a whole PAN column** when tokenization with preserved joins would remove it from scope.
- **Putting an LLM behind only a network firewall.** Prompt injection arrives in perfectly legitimate HTTPS requests.
- **Launching Model Armor in block mode untested.** Tune in inspect-only mode first.
- **Leaving every Model Garden model deployable** in production projects, or relying on private networking while the AI APIs stay publicly reachable outside a perimeter.
- **Counting audit logs, VPC-SC or CMEK as erasure**, or deleting from production only while exports, caches and backups keep the subject.
- **Destroying a shared CMEK key** for one person's request: it erases everyone under it.
- **Archiving personal data indefinitely**, or locking retention on a bucket that holds erasable personal data.
- **Preparing evidence only before the audit**, or leaving audit logs at 30-day `_Default` retention for a year-long review period.

## Exam tips

- **Provider cert is not your cert:** Google's SOC 2 covers its infrastructure; you still need your own SOC 2 for your application and operations.
- **HIPAA recipe:** sign the BAA, use only covered services, enable Data Access logs, protect with CMEK and least privilege; keep PHI out of labels and metadata.
- **PCI scope reduction:** Sensitive Data Protection de-identification with format-preserving tokenization using KMS-wrapped keys; tokens still support analytics joins.
- **GDPR:** DPA plus location constraints, and Sensitive Data Protection discovery to find personal data for access and erasure requests.
- **Sovereignty with personnel controls:** Assured Workloads (for example EU Regions and Support) plus `gcp.resourceLocations`; the constraint alone is not a residency commitment.
- **SAIF:** a framework, not a product. Six elements (foundations, detection and response, automation, harmonized platform controls, adaptive controls, business-context risk); map them to IAM, VPC-SC and Org Policy, SCC with AI Protection, and Model Armor.
- **SAIF risk map:** four components (data, infrastructure, model, application); assurance and governance controls apply to every risk.
- **Gen-AI prompt and response protection:** Model Armor, optionally with Sensitive Data Protection; tune in inspect-only mode first and use floor settings for org baselines.
- **Private AI deployment:** VPC-SC perimeter plus Private Service Connect endpoints, CMEK (which does not cover metadata or other services), and `vertexai.allowedModels` for an approved-model list.
- **Ownership and COPPA:** customer data is yours and used only per contract, but you are the controller and the COPPA operator; the provider cannot certify it for you.
- **Erasure:** a verified request means deletion or anonymization in every store, including copies, exports, caches and backups. Audit logs, VPC-SC and CMEK alone do not satisfy it.
- **Storage limitation:** per-category retention with automated deletion (lifecycle, TTL, expiration), not an indefinite archive. Mind soft delete, time travel and backup windows.
- **Legal retention beats erasure:** records under a statutory duty or hold are kept, restricted, then deleted. Keep erasable data out of locked buckets.
- **Crypto-shredding:** destroying a key erases everything under it, so it fits per-tenant keys, not a shared key for one subject.
- **SOC 2 Type II evidence:** immutable, restricted audit sinks and SCC posture reporting support audits, but must show controls operating across the period (locked-retention audit sink, exported SCC history, asset snapshots, review and pipeline records); a point-in-time report is not enough.
